The glass cylinder contains water. When the temperature of the water changes, so does its density.
Each bulb has a label printed with a temperature, as shown in Fig. 4.1. The bulbs have different
densities. At 21 °C, only bulb A is at the bottom of the cylinder.

mark_scheme.label: 4(a)
mark_scheme.text:
Density of bulb A greater than the density of the water (and sinks)
Density of other bulbs less than the density of water (and float)

content.html: Explain, in terms of density, why bulb A is at the bottom of the cylinder and the other bulbs are floating.
content.text: Explain, in terms of density, why bulb A is at the bottom of the cylinder and the other bulbs are floating.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The temperature of the surrounding air increases to a temperature above 23 °C.

mark_scheme.label: 4(b)(i)
mark_scheme.text:
Glass is a poor conductor of heat OR glass conducts heat at a slow rate
OR water has a high (specific) heat capacity

content.html: Suggest one reason why there is a delay before the temperature of the water increases to 23 °C.

mark_scheme.label: 4(b)(ii)
mark_scheme.text:
The water expands OR separation of water molecules increases
The water becomes less dense
Bulb B now has a greater density than the water (and sinks) OR Weight of bulb B more than buoyancy forces / upthrust

content.html: Explain why, after this delay, bulb B sinks. Assume the bulbs do not expand.
